subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage: I'm Pradeep, and I sit opposite Siddharth in the Leeds office. At the team lunch on Wednesday, two colleagues took turns imitating how he says "schedule," and laughed. He smiled thinly and ate faster. Afterwards nobody invited him to the pub, as usual. I couldn't tell how much it hurt; he only said, "It's a bit tiring." On Friday he asked one of them, calmly, in the corridor, to stop the impressions. The colleague shrugged it off, and it happened again. Siddharth wrote it down with dates and sent it to HR. Then he joined the Saturday five-a-side that some of us play. "Their bias isn't my flaw," he told me, almost to himself, "but I still have to make it stop."

qa.q: What did the two colleagues imitate at the team lunch?
What might Siddharth have felt during the lunch, given his thin smile and how fast he ate?
qa.a: He may have been hurt and tried to hide it, but Pradeep couldn't tell how much it hurt. A smile is a cue, not proof.

qa.q: What did Siddharth do after the impressions happened again, and why does it help?
qa.a: He wrote it down with dates and sent it to HR, so there is a record for a proper report. He also found friendlier company at the five-a-side.

qa.q: How might the colleague who shrugged it off have seen the impressions?
qa.a: Possibly as a harmless joke, although Siddharth clearly experienced it as mockery. The repeat suggests the request wasn't taken seriously.

grounding: Stereotypes and accent mockery in a new country; naming it, calmly asking for it to stop, finding supportive people and reporting discrimination.

subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage:
In his third week at the Gurugram insurance office, Jeevan heard it again. At the coffee machine, a colleague put on a thick Kannada accent: "Yenri, sir, coffee strong-aa?" Two others laughed.

Jeevan laughed along, then went back to his desk and stared at the same spreadsheet for twenty minutes. He had topped his university. Here, he'd started talking less in meetings.

Mahima, from claims, pulled up a chair at lunch. "That coffee thing. It happens to you a lot, doesn't it?"

He nodded. Saying it out loud made his throat tight. "I thought maybe I was being too sensitive."

"You're not. It's mockery."

The next time it happened, Jeevan said evenly, "Please don't imitate my accent. It's not funny to me." The colleague rolled his eyes but stopped. When it started up again a week later, Jeevan and Mahima wrote it up for HR together.

That evening, on the phone to his mother, he spoke in Kannada for an hour, and didn't lower his voice.

qa.q: What did the colleague say in a put-on accent?
What was Jeevan feeling as he stared at the spreadsheet?
qa.a: He felt hurt and shaken, starting to doubt himself and speak less in meetings.

qa.q: Which of Jeevan's steps helped most, and why?
qa.a: Naming it with Mahima, asking the colleague calmly to stop, and reporting to HR when it continued, because each step treated the bias as the problem, not himself.

qa.q: How does Mahima see what is happening to Jeevan?
qa.a: Mahima sees it clearly as mockery and wants him to know he is not being too sensitive.

grounding: The passage shows a newcomer facing accent mockery at work, naming it, finding a supportive colleague, addressing it calmly and reporting it.

subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage:
Dear Trisha,

You asked how Melbourne really is. Mostly good. But I want to tell you something I haven't told Amma.

In my share house, one of the flatmates keeps saying things like, "You people must love spicy food, right?" and "Your English is so good for an Indian." Last week they had a barbecue and didn't invite me. I heard it through my wall.

I cried, then felt stupid for crying. Then I started wondering if my English actually was bad.

It isn't. I know that now. My lab partner, who's from Chile, sat with me and said, "They've decided who you are before meeting you. That's their problem." I've started eating dinners with her and her friends.

I also told my flatmate, calmly, that the comments aren't compliments. The landlord knows about it too, in writing, in case it gets worse.

Write back soon. I miss your laugh.

Jaya

qa.q: What did the flatmate say about Jaya's English?
qa.a: "Your English is so good for an Indian."

qa.q: How did Jaya feel after hearing the barbecue through the wall?
qa.a: Jaya felt hurt and left out, then foolish for crying, and began to doubt Jaya's own English.

qa.q: What steps did Jaya take, and why were they wise?
qa.a: Jaya found supportive friends, told the flatmate calmly that the comments weren't compliments, and put the problem in writing to the landlord, treating the bias as the flatmate's problem.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Trisha may feel protective and sad for Jaya, but proud of how calmly Jaya handled it.

grounding: The letter shows someone in a new country facing stereotypes and exclusion, naming the hurt, finding supportive people, addressing it calmly and putting a report in writing.
